title: Reliability pillar (recover from failure)
hook: Reliability means a workload performs its intended function correctly and consistently — including when components fail. Design for failure across Availability Zones (AZs), regions, and dependencies.

blocks.text: Principles: automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, manage change through automation, and anticipate failure. Patterns: Multi-AZ RDS, Auto Scaling groups, health checks, backups with tested restore, chaos engineering, and defined Recovery Time Objective (RTO) / Recovery Point Objective (RPO).

entries.plainDefinition: Resources span isolated AZs within a region

entries.example: Terminate random ECS task in Game Day

blocks.text: Interviewers ask "what happens when an AZ goes down?" and "have you tested backup restore?" Reliability HRIs — single-AZ databases, no auto scaling, untested DR — fail enterprise due diligence.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: design for failure, Multi-AZ, auto scaling, backup/restore tested, defined RTO/RPO.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Eliminate single points of failure
items.body: Multi-AZ for data and compute; no one NAT gateway for all egress if critical.

items.title: Auto scale and health check
items.body: Replace unhealthy targets; scale on demand metrics.

items.title: Backup and restore
items.body: Automated backups; quarterly restore drill with documented RTO.

items.title: Plan for region failure
items.body: Active-passive or active-active multi-region if RTO requires it.

diagram.title: Failure domains
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  REG[Region] --> AZ1[AZ-a app]
  REG --> AZ2[AZ-b app]
  AZ1 --> RDS[(Multi-AZ RDS)]
  AZ2 --> RDS

snippet.label: Multi-AZ RDS
snippet.code:
Database:
  Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
  Properties:
    MultiAZ: true
    BackupRetentionPeriod: 14
    DeletionProtection: true
snippet.explanation: Automatic failover to standby AZ on primary failure.

snippet.label: ASG across AZs
snippet.code:
AutoScalingGroup:
  Properties:
    MinSize: 2
    MaxSize: 10
    VPCZoneIdentifier:
      - !Ref Az1Subnet
      - !Ref Az2Subnet
    HealthCheckType: ELB
snippet.explanation: Horizontal scale across AZs with ELB health checks.

snippet.label: Restore test
snippet.explanation: Prove RTO — untested backups are wishful thinking.

snippet.label: Route53 failover
snippet.code:
PrimaryRecord:
  Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
  Properties:
    Failover: PRIMARY
    HealthCheckId: !Ref PrimaryHealthCheck
    SetIdentifier: primary

rows: PM2 cluster on one VM — weaker

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Single-AZ production database. Backups enabled but never restored. One NAT Gateway for all private subnets — AZ failure blocks egress.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: last successful restore drill date; AZ failure Game Day results; SLO burn rate alerts; chaos experiment pass rate.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "we are in the cloud so it is reliable" — rejected. Strong answer: explicit failure modes, Multi-AZ, tested restore, defined RTO/RPO.

interviewTakeaways: Reliability = perform correctly under failure; design for AZ/region/dependency loss.
Untested backups are not backups — schedule restore drills.
Multi-AZ RDS fails over automatically; apps must handle DNS/cache staleness.
60s: Multi-AZ, auto scaling, health checks, backup with tested restore, RTO/RPO. Chaos Game Days prove it. Cloud does not auto-heal bad design.
Follow-up: RTO 15 min — active-active or failover?
commonPitfalls: Single-AZ prod DB — classic HRI and interview fail.
Strong answer: Multi-AZ, ASG, tested restore, defined RTO/RPO with tradeoff cost.
One NAT GW for all AZs — AZ outage kills egress.
No health checks on custom app port.

jsTsCorrelations.note: aws-sdk v3 retry strategy handles transient failures — app must still handle throttling.
opossum or similar pattern for dependency failure — Reliability at app layer.
